title: Unilateral delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy: a case report
case_prompt:
An 81-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia and chronic kidney disease (stage G2), hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for cytoreductive therapy. On hospital day 13, he suddenly developed right-sided hemiparesis and global aphasia (NIHSS score 17). Noncontrast head CT showed no early ischemic changes (ASPECTS 10), and CT angiography demonstrated an occlusion of the left cervical internal carotid artery without intracranial large-vessel occlusion. He was transferred for endovascular therapy under general anesthesia. Angiography revealed a subpetrous dissection of the left internal carotid artery; aspiration thrombectomy achieved complete reperfusion (eTICI 3) with an onset-to-recanalization time of 265 minutes. 

After extubation, his aphasia and hemiparesis improved immediately. Twenty-four–hour NCCT showed neither infarction nor hemorrhage. On day 2 after treatment, his NIHSS score was 5. On day 10, MRI showed no diffusion-weighted or FLAIR abnormalities, and MR angiography confirmed no reocclusion. 

In the subsequent days, the patient’s speech fluidity, comprehension, and praxis gradually worsened, and he was readmitted on day 23 (NIHSS 7). Routine labs and EEG were unremarkable. Repeat MRI demonstrated no diffusion restriction or ADC changes but revealed new, subtle, homogeneous FLAIR hyperintensities confined to the left anterior and middle cerebral artery white matter, sparing the cortex and subcortical U-fibers.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute ischemic stroke recurrence — “following acute ischemic stroke or manifest hypoxic brain damage, FLAIR hyperintensities should have already been visible on first MRI imaging on day 10 and not developed later to be visible on MR imaging on day 23.”  
2. Global hypoxic–ischemic injury — “Typical for global hypoxic-ischemic injury is increased signal intensity on DWI in cerebellar hemispheres, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex.”  
3. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome — “In PRES patchy T2/FLAIR hyperintensities sparing the cortex and usually located in parieto-occipital lobes … our patient did not have any hypertensive phases and did not show any kind of intracranial hemorrhage on imaging…”  
4. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — “PML … hyperintensities … often involving subcortical U-fibers … However, the U-fibers were spared in our patient. In addition, the anatomical distribution … makes DPHL more likely and isolated PML in this area less likely.”  
5. Status epilepticus–related changes — “In status epilepticus, T2/FLAIR hyperintensities … are usually accompanied by acutely restricted diffusion. … In our case, clinical course, imaging appearance, and EEG pattern … did not match these differential diagnoses.”  
6. Metabolic or toxic leukoencephalopathy — “Metabolic or toxic disorders … would, if any, have caused more global, symmetrical changes on MR imaging, which is why they are not discussed further …”
